key: B♭ major; ending in D major
intro: Fritz Mahler and the Hartford Symphony Orchestra play Copland’s wartime Fanfare for the Common Man. Timpani, bass drum and tam-tam open it before the trumpets enter, and the rising trumpet calls end on an unexpected D major chord.

sections.label: A · Trumpet fanfare in rising intervals
A′ · Fanfare theme, full brass
sections.mNote: Longer descending phrases between the rising calls.

cues.title: Percussion opening and trumpet entry
cues.text: Timpani, bass drum and tam-tam open the piece with strokes separated by silence. The trumpets then enter with a figure that rises in two short notes and a long one. Copland uses both the percussion strokes and the rising trumpet figure throughout the piece.
cues.evidence: Jennifer DeLapp-Birkett, “What Makes Copland’s Fanfare for the Common Man Uncommon?” (2023), describes the percussion opening and the short-short-long trumpet figure, with examples from bars 1–12. https://www.aaroncopland.com/news/midday-thoughts-what-makes-coplands-fanfare-for-the-common-man-uncommon/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rising and descending figures
cues.text: The rising calls alternate with evenly paced notes moving downwards. The descending phrases grow longer as more of the brass joins, with extended passages in bars 26–34 and 36–40. The short rising flourish recurs between the heavier descending passages.
cues.evidence: DeLapp-Birkett’s analysis distinguishes the rising flourish from the descending, evenly paced figure and traces their expansion through the piece. Her table identifies the extended descending passages in bars 26–34 and 36–40. The Los Angeles Philharmonic’s programme note has three unison trumpets present the theme, in a score for four horns, three trumpets, three trombones and tuba. https://www.aaroncopland.com/news/midday-thoughts-what-makes-coplands-fanfare-for-the-common-man-uncommon/ https://www.hollywoodbowl.com/musicdb/pieces/345/fanfare-for-the-common-man
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chord in D major
cues.text: At the end the rising call slows into three weighty notes. The music has centred on B♭ for most of its length. The final chord is D major.
cues.evidence: DeLapp-Birkett identifies the slowed final flourish and the concluding D-major triad after the predominantly B♭-centred music. https://www.aaroncopland.com/news/midday-thoughts-what-makes-coplands-fanfare-for-the-common-man-uncommon/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Modernist composer from Brooklyn, known for his open fifths, his cowboy dances and a slow fanfare for brass.

composer.background:
The Copland family lived above and beside their department store on Washington Avenue in Brooklyn. Aaron, born on 14 November 1900, was the youngest of Sarah and Harris Copland’s five children. His parents were Russian-born Jewish immigrants, and everyone in the family helped in the shop. His sister Laurine gave him his first piano lessons. When he wanted professional lessons, his parents let him find a teacher and agreed to pay. By 1917 he was crossing the Brooklyn Bridge to study harmony and counterpoint with Rubin Goldmark.

At Fontainebleau in 1921 a friend persuaded him to sit in on Nadia Boulanger’s harmony class. She became his composition teacher, and the year he had planned to spend abroad stretched to three. In Paris he encountered Stravinsky’s music and heard the latest concert works. Boulanger took him to meet Serge Koussevitzky, who was about to take over the Boston Symphony Orchestra. After the visit Koussevitzky commissioned a symphony with Boulanger herself as organ soloist.
